passage:
When I was in Class 4, I told everyone my uncle was on television every week. He isn't. He fixes televisions. I also said I came first in class, but I was ninth.
Thomas had just joined, and everyone crowded around him because he had lived in Kenya and owned a real telescope. Nobody crowded around me. So I got louder.
One day Thomas asked, "Irfan, can I meet your TV uncle?" My tummy went cold. I said he was busy. Thomas just said, "Okay. Do you want to see my telescope on Saturday?" He liked me anyway. I felt silly about all the shouting.
I still like being noticed. Now I try to be noticed for true things.

qa.q: What does Irfan's uncle really do?
qa.a: He fixes televisions.

qa.q: Why did Irfan get louder after Thomas joined?
qa.a: Irfan felt overlooked because everyone crowded around Thomas, and wanted to be seen as special too.

qa.q: What small step could help Irfan feel noticed without boasting?
qa.a: Irfan could share real interests, the way Thomas shared his telescope, so classmates notice true things.

qa.q: How might Thomas have seen Irfan's big stories?
qa.a: Thomas didn't seem to mind them; he just wanted a friend, which is why he invited Irfan to see the telescope anyway.

grounding: A child looks back on boasting about a relative and a rank because being overlooked felt frightening, and learns Irfan was liked without it.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 5C, Wednesday.
Keerthana has told the class three times this week that she is "going to be head girl, definitely", that her cousin is a pilot, and that her new pencil box cost more than anyone's. Each time she speaks louder and watches faces. When nobody reacts, she starts again.
Today in art she held up her drawing and said, "Mine is the best one, right?" before anyone had looked. Her other hand was gripping the desk.
I think she worries that without the big claims she'll disappear. After class I asked her to help set up the reading corner, and told her that her lettering on the posters is careful and clear. She beamed, and didn't boast once in the next period.
Rafiq Hussain

qa.q: What did Keerthana say about her new pencil box?
qa.a: She said her new pencil box cost more than anyone's.

qa.q: What does Keerthana's hand gripping the desk suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt anxious and hungry for approval, worried that without big claims she might go unnoticed.

qa.q: Which step by the teacher helped, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq gave her a real job and specific praise for her careful lettering, so she felt noticed without needing to boast.

qa.q: How might the other children see Keerthana's claims?
qa.a: They may tune out or feel pushed aside, which is why nobody reacted and she kept starting again.

grounding: A teacher notices a girl's loud boasting about rank, a relative and belongings, and reads it as a fear of being ordinary.

passage:
Class teacher's diary, Grade 5, second week of term.
Dolma joined us from another town this month. At lunch today she told the table her uncle is famous and is on TV every night. Yesterday it was a room full of remote-control cars.
Leela rolled her eyes and moved to another table. Dolma saw it. She ate the rest of her lunch looking at her tiffin, and her voice got even louder when the next child sat down.
I don't think Dolma is trying to trick anyone. I think she is worried no one will notice her here.
After lunch I asked her to hand out the art paper, and I asked about her old school's garden, which she described beautifully. Leela listened too. Tomorrow I'll pair Dolma and Leela for the plant project.

qa.q: What did Dolma say her uncle does?
qa.a: She said her uncle is famous and is on TV every night.

qa.q: What does Dolma's louder voice after Leela left suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Dolma felt rejected and anxious, and pushed harder for admiration because she was afraid of being overlooked.

qa.q: How did the teacher support Dolma?
qa.a: The teacher gave her a helpful job and asked about something real, her old school's garden, so she could be noticed without boasting.

qa.q: How does Leela see Dolma's boasting?
qa.a: Leela finds it annoying and rolls her eyes, though she listens when Dolma talks about the real garden.

grounding: A teacher's diary shows a new child boasting about a famous uncle and toys, pointing to a fear of being overlooked rather than a plan to trick.

passage:
Thursday
Today I, Parul, told Pooja and her friends three times that I came first in the drawing competition. The first time they said "wow." The second time Pooja said, "Yes, you told us." The third time nobody said anything, and Pooja went to play hopscotch with the others.
I don't know why I kept saying it. It is true. I did come first. But when they said wow, I felt big, and when they stopped, I felt small again, so I said it again.
Mummy says I don't need a medal to be liked. But at the new school nobody knows me yet. Pooja has had the same friends since nursery. If I'm not the drawing-first girl, what am I?
Tomorrow maybe I'll just ask if I can play hopscotch.

qa.q: How many times did Parul tell Pooja and her friends about the drawing competition?
qa.a: Parul told them three times.

qa.q: Why did Parul keep repeating the news?
qa.a: Parul felt small and afraid of being ordinary at the new school, and the "wow" made her feel big for a moment.

qa.q: What small step does Parul plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: She plans to simply ask if she can play hopscotch, joining in instead of trying to be admired.

qa.q: What is it like for Pooja to hear the same boast three times?
qa.a: Pooja feels bored and a bit annoyed, so she goes to play hopscotch with the others.

grounding: A child's diary shows repeated boasting about a win as an urgent need to feel worthy and a fear of being overlooked.

passage:
The new cycle arrived on a Sunday, red with a silver bell, and by Monday every child in the village knew about it, because Uday rode it past the well ten times.
"It has gears," he told the boys by the banyan tree. "My chacha sent it from the city. It's the fastest in the whole district."
Siddharth, who walked two kilometres to school every day, said nothing. He just watched.
At lunchtime, Uday started again. "Nobody else has a cycle like this. Nobody."
Siddharth finally said, "Can I ride it?"
Uday opened his mouth to say no, then saw the other boys looking away, bored. His throat felt tight. Without the cycle, he was just Uday, the boy who came last in races.
"Okay," he said. "One round."
Siddharth rode it round the well, grinning, and for a moment Uday forgot to boast.

qa.q: Where did Uday ride the new cycle ten times?
qa.a: He rode it past the well.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he saw the boys looking away?
qa.a: Uday felt anxious and small, afraid that without the cycle he was just the boy who came last in races.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than boasting, and why?
qa.a: Letting Siddharth ride it worked, because sharing brought real connection and made Uday forget to boast.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth to hear Uday's boasting?
qa.a: Siddharth, who walks two kilometres to school, quietly watches and probably feels left out, until Uday lets him ride.

grounding: It shows a village child boasting about a new cycle out of an urgent need to feel worthy and fear of being ordinary.

passage:
In his first week at a new school in Singapore, Wei told everyone at lunch that his uncle owned the biggest restaurant in the city, that he had the newest game console before anyone, and that he had been top of his old class in maths.
Yosef, sitting across from him, asked, "Which restaurant?"
Wei named one he'd seen on a bus advertisement. Yosef's eyebrows went up. His mum worked there. She'd never heard of any uncle.
After school Yosef found Wei alone by the gate, kicking a stone.
"You don't have to say all that stuff," Yosef said. "I just wanted to know if you like football."
Wei's cheeks went red. "At my old school, nobody noticed me unless I had something big."
"Well, we have practice on Thursday," Yosef said. "Nobody's big there. We're all bad."
Wei laughed for the first time that week.

qa.q: What did Wei say his uncle owned?
qa.a: The biggest restaurant in the city.

qa.q: Why did Wei boast so much in his first week?
qa.a: Wei was afraid of being overlooked, since at the old school nobody noticed him unless he had something big.

qa.q: What did Yosef do that helped Wei?
qa.a: He found Wei alone, said the boasting wasn't needed, and invited him to Thursday football practice, offering belonging without conditions.

qa.q: How might Yosef have felt hearing about the restaurant?
qa.a: Yosef was surprised and doubtful, since his mum worked there and had never heard of the uncle, but chose kindness over exposing Wei.

grounding: Shows a new child boasting about a rich uncle and top marks out of fear of being overlooked, and a classmate offering simple belonging.
